Chapter 2: Work Physiology

IPE 407 — Ergonomics & Safety Management  |  RAS (Sanim Sir)  |  Exam Importance: ★★★★★

Overview

Work physiology quantifies the body's response to physical work — oxygen demand, heart rate, energy expenditure — to set safe workload limits. It is the most heavily examined RAS topic. Key concepts: oxygen debt, BMR, MAP, Murrell's formula for rest periods, and physiological strain measurement methods.

★★★★★ Top Topics: (1) Factors affecting energy consumption during work — 2× exam. (2) Measuring physiological strain (methods, advantages/disadvantages) — 2× exam. (3) Maximum aerobic power (MAP) — 2× exam. Know all three cold.

Oxygen, Energy & BMR ★★★★ Exam

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)

BMR = minimum energy required to maintain vital functions at complete rest. Measured in kcal/day or W.

  • Average: ~1500–1800 kcal/day for adult males; ~1200–1400 for females
  • BMR measured at: complete rest, post-absorptive state (12h fasting), comfortable temperature, awake

Factors Affecting BMR

PYQ 2021-22 Q1a (15 marks): Explain oxygen debt, EPOC, BMR, and factors affecting BMR.
  • Body size: Larger body surface area → higher BMR (more tissue to maintain)
  • Age: BMR decreases ~2% per decade after age 20 (muscle mass declines)
  • Sex: Males have ~5–10% higher BMR (greater lean muscle mass)
  • Body composition: Muscle tissue is more metabolically active than fat → more lean mass = higher BMR
  • Hormones: Thyroid hormones (T₃, T₄) are primary regulators — hyperthyroidism ↑ BMR, hypothyroidism ↓ BMR
  • Temperature: Cold increases BMR (shivering thermogenesis); fever raises BMR ~7% per 1°C
  • Nutritional state: Starvation/fasting lowers BMR (conservation response)
  • Stress/epinephrine: Adrenaline → ↑ heart rate, ↑ metabolic rate → ↑ BMR

Oxygen Debt & EPOC

  • Oxygen debt (classical): The extra O₂ consumed after exercise above resting level, to "repay" the O₂ deficit incurred during intense work. Originally thought to repay lactate.
  • EPOC (Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption): Modern term. Elevated O₂ consumption after exercise for many reasons beyond just lactate clearance:
    • Lactate conversion back to glycogen (Cori cycle in liver)
    • Replenishing ATP and PCr stores in muscle
    • Elevated body temperature → higher metabolic rate
    • Elevated circulating catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)
    • Increased ventilation and cardiac work during recovery
    • Muscle repair and protein synthesis after the exercise bout
PYQ 2023-24 Q5b (5 marks): What is the purpose of extra oxygen intake after intense physical activity?

Extra O₂ intake after intense exercise (EPOC) serves to: (1) Replenish O₂ stores in myoglobin and hemoglobin; (2) Resynthesize ATP and PCr; (3) Oxidize accumulated lactate; (4) Support elevated body temperature, ventilation, and cardiac output during recovery; (5) Drive protein synthesis for muscle repair.

Anaerobic Threshold (AT)

The exercise intensity above which lactate accumulates faster than it can be cleared. Beyond AT, work duration is limited. AT ≈ 50–60% of VO₂max in untrained; 70–80% in trained workers. Important for setting sustainable workload limits.

Cardiovascular & Respiratory Response ★★★★ Exam

PYQ 2022-23 Q1a (15 marks): Describe the respiratory and cardiovascular responses to physical activity with necessary diagrams.

Heart Rate Response

  • Resting HR: ~70 bpm; maximum HR: ~220 − age (bpm)
  • HR increases linearly with work intensity up to VO₂max
  • Recovery: HR returns to resting — rate depends on fitness level
Heart rate recovery curve — slope reflects fitness level

Heart Rate Recovery Curve

PYQ 2015-16 Q4b (8 marks): Explain the heart rate recovery curve and its relationship with work posture and energy consumption.
  • After work stops, HR drops rapidly at first, then more slowly (exponential decay)
  • Faster recovery = higher fitness / lower physiological strain
  • Brouha's criterion: If HR at 1 min post-work > 110 bpm, work is too heavy
  • Work posture: Awkward postures (stooped, arms overhead) increase HR even at same external load because more muscles must co-contract for stabilization → higher energy cost

Cardiac Output & Blood Distribution

PYQ 2018-19 Q4b (5 marks): How does blood distribution in the skin change during heavy work vs rest?
  • At rest: Blood distributed to organs, muscle, skin, brain roughly equally based on metabolic need
  • During heavy work: Cardiovascular system diverts blood flow: active muscles receive ~80–85% of cardiac output (up from ~15–20% at rest); skin blood flow INCREASES (for heat dissipation via radiation/convection); gastrointestinal and renal flow DECREASES; cardiac output rises from ~5 L/min at rest to ~20–25 L/min during maximal exercise
  • Conflict at high temperature: Both muscles AND skin need blood → limits exercise performance in heat
PYQ 2015-16 Q4c (10 marks): Passage correction on blood distribution during work — the typical error is saying skin blood flow DECREASES during heavy work. It actually INCREASES (for thermoregulation) until thermal stress is so extreme the body prioritizes muscle over skin.

Respiratory Response

  • Ventilation rises from ~6 L/min at rest to ~100–150 L/min at max exercise
  • VO₂ (oxygen uptake) increases linearly with work intensity up to VO₂max
  • VCO₂ / VO₂ ratio = Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER): ~0.7 at rest (fat oxidation), ~1.0 at anaerobic threshold, >1.0 above threshold (CO₂ from bicarbonate buffering of lactate)

Measuring Physiological Strain ★★★★★ 2× Exam

PYQ 2020-21/2014-15 (★ 2×): Describe the means of measuring physiological strain during work. Discuss advantages and disadvantages. (15/20 marks)

1. Heart Rate (HR) Measurement

AspectDetail
MethodChest strap HR monitor, ECG, pulse oximeter
AdvantagesNon-invasive, continuous, easy to use in field, good proxy for cardiovascular strain, well-validated reference ranges
DisadvantagesAffected by emotion, heat, dehydration (not purely work effort); high inter-individual variability; can't distinguish muscle group involvement
PYQ 2013-14 Q7a (10 marks): Problems associated with measuring heart rate as a physiological strain indicator.
  • Affected by environmental temperature (heat → higher HR even at same work rate)
  • Caffeine, medication, stress, anxiety inflate HR
  • Acclimatization: a fit worker shows same HR for harder work — normative values may be misleading
  • Static/isometric work (gripping, squeezing) causes disproportionate HR rise vs dynamic work at same oxygen cost
  • Not specific to muscle groups — can't locate which body region is overloaded

2. Oxygen Consumption (VO₂)

AspectDetail
MethodExpired gas analysis (Douglas bag, metabolic cart, portable spirometer)
AdvantagesDirect measure of energy expenditure; not affected by emotion/stress; gold standard for work capacity
DisadvantagesCumbersome equipment; restricts natural movement; requires lab conditions; not suitable for all jobs (dusty/wet environments)

3. Electromyography (EMG)

PYQ Jan 2021 Q6a (8 marks): Explain electromyography and the relationship between muscular strain, workload and work rate.
AspectDetail
MethodSurface electrodes detect motor unit electrical activity; needle EMG for deeper muscles
AdvantagesLocalizes specific muscle effort; detects onset of fatigue; shows static loading invisible to other methods
DisadvantagesSignal affected by electrode placement, skin impedance, crosstalk from adjacent muscles; requires calibration per individual; not simple to interpret in field

EMG–Workload relationship: EMG amplitude (RMS) increases linearly with muscle force up to MVC (maximum voluntary contraction). At the same force level, as work rate increases, EMG frequency shifts (median frequency decreases — EMG fatigue indicator). Prolonged static contraction at >10–15% MVC leads to rapid fatigue.

4. Lactic Acid (Blood Lactate)

AspectDetail
MethodFinger-prick blood sample; lactate analyzer
AdvantagesDirectly indicates anaerobic metabolism; defines anaerobic threshold (4 mmol/L threshold)
DisadvantagesInvasive; discontinuous; lag between muscle lactate and blood lactate; not suitable for field use

5. Perceived Exertion (Borg Scale)

  • Borg's RPE scale: 6–20 (correlates with HR/10 approximately)
  • Simple, non-invasive, subjective but valid indicator of physiological load
  • Useful when equipment is unavailable; widely used in occupational health

Factors Affecting Energy Consumption ★★★★★ 2× Exam

PYQ 2023-24/2011-12 (★ 2×) Q7b/Q2b: What are the factors affecting energy consumption during work? (20/10 marks)

Task-Related Factors

  • Workload (force × displacement): Primary determinant — heavier loads, faster movements = more energy
  • Work rate: Energy expenditure is non-linear — doubling speed more than doubles energy cost (especially for walking, cycling)
  • Work posture: Awkward postures (stooped, kneeling, overhead work) increase energy cost by 15–50% vs neutral posture — more muscles co-contracting for stabilization
  • Type of contraction: Dynamic (isotonic) is more efficient than static (isometric) work at same force level; eccentric work uses less O₂ than concentric
  • Muscle groups involved: Large muscle group work (legs) is more efficient than small muscle group work (arms) for the same external power output
  • Tool/equipment design: Poorly designed tools increase force requirements → higher energy expenditure

Worker-Related Factors

  • Body weight: Heavier workers expend more energy for weight-bearing tasks (walking, climbing); weight-independent for arm tasks
  • Fitness level: Trained workers: same external work at lower %VO₂max → more efficient; lower steady-state HR and O₂ consumption
  • Age: VO₂max declines ~1% per year after age 25 → same task represents higher % of capacity
  • Sex: Women have lower absolute VO₂max (~10–20% lower) but similar relative capacity at same % body weight; different muscle mass distribution
  • Skill/experience: Skilled workers use less energy for same task (better coordination, reduced co-contraction)
  • Acclimatization: Heat-acclimatized workers: lower core temperature rise, HR response at same external work

Environmental Factors

  • Temperature: Heat → increased HR and ventilation for same work; cold → shivering thermogenesis adds metabolic cost
  • Altitude: Lower O₂ partial pressure → higher ventilation, higher HR for same work → lower aerobic capacity
  • Humidity: High humidity impairs heat dissipation → higher skin blood flow competing with muscle → apparent higher physiological cost

Rest Periods & Shift Work ★★★★ Exam

Murrell's Formula for Rest Periods

PYQ 2015-16 Q4a (7 marks) [NUMERICAL]: Calculate rest period for a task with 8 kcal/min using Figure 4(a) and Murrell's formula.
R = T × (W − S) / (W − 1.5)

Where: R = required rest time (minutes) T = total work time (minutes) W = average energy expenditure of work task (kcal/min) S = standard (acceptable) energy expenditure = 5 kcal/min (Murrell) or as given 1.5 = resting metabolic rate (kcal/min)

If W ≤ S, no rest is needed (work is within acceptable limit). The formula ensures total energy expenditure over T + R minutes does not exceed the standard.

PYQ 2023-24 Q7c [NUMERICAL] (5 marks): Calculate required rest for a 120-minute shift. Work involves tasks at 5.9, 6.8, 3.9, 1.5 kcal/min; use Murrell's formula (S = 5 kcal/min). Provide step-by-step solution.
Approach: (1) Find weighted average W for the shift. (2) Apply Murrell's: R = T(W−S)/(W−1.5). If W < S, check each sub-task individually.

For a mixed task, average W = (5.9+6.8+3.9+1.5)/4 = 18.1/4 = 4.525 kcal/min. Since W (4.525) < S (5), technically no rest required by Murrell's standard. But the problem likely wants sub-task breakdown — apply separately for heavy tasks (5.9 and 6.8) over their durations.

Numerical: 2010-11 Q1c (10 marks)

PYQ 2010-11 Q1c: Worker lifts 20 kg, 15 times/hour, height 40 to 60 inches (20 inch rise). Energy = 4 g-cal/ft-lb. Calculate energy expenditure per minute.
Solution:
Work per lift = F × d = (20 kg × 2.205 lb/kg) × (20 in × 1/12 ft/in) = 44.1 lb × 1.667 ft = 73.5 ft-lb
Energy per lift = 73.5 ft-lb × 4 g-cal/ft-lb = 294 g-cal = 0.294 kcal
Lifts per minute = 15/60 = 0.25
Energy rate = 0.294 × 0.25 = 0.0735 kcal/min from the lifting task
(Add basal metabolism ~1.5 kcal/min for total work metabolic rate)
Note: Exact answer depends on problem statement units; this approach demonstrates the method.

Maximum Aerobic Power (MAP)

PYQ 2013-14/2010-11 (★ 2×) Q7c/Q6c: What is Maximum Aerobic Power (MAP)? How is it related to age and sex? (15/5 marks)
  • MAP = VO₂max = maximum rate of O₂ utilization; the ceiling of aerobic capacity
  • Measured in mL O₂/kg/min or L O₂/min
  • Typical values: Sedentary male ~35–45 mL/kg/min; Trained ~55–70 mL/kg/min; Elite ~80+ mL/kg/min; Females ~10–20% lower
  • Age: VO₂max peaks at ~20–25 years; declines ~1% per year after 25 (due to lower max HR, reduced stroke volume, decreased muscle mass)
  • Sex: Males have higher MAP due to: greater cardiac output (stroke volume), lower body fat %, higher hemoglobin concentration, larger muscle mass

Practical limit: Sustained work should not exceed 33% of VO₂max (1/3 rule) for an 8-hour shift to prevent cumulative fatigue.

Shift Work & Overtime Effects

PYQ 2015-16/2013-14 (★ 2×): How do overtime and shift work influence worker efficiency? (10 marks)
  • Night shift: Disrupts circadian rhythm → impaired alertness, slower reaction time, higher error rate; core body temperature lowest at ~4–5 AM when night shift workers are most vulnerable
  • Rotating shifts: Constant circadian disruption → chronic sleep debt → reduced cognitive and physical performance; GI problems, cardiovascular disease risk
  • Overtime: Fatigue accumulates → productivity per hour decreases after 48–50 hours/week (output drops even as input hours rise)
  • Efficiency curve: Worker efficiency ~100% for 1–4 hours; starts to decline from 5–6 hours due to physiological fatigue; returns during breaks; cumulative effect over days if inadequate recovery

Muscle Spasm vs Muscle Cramp

PYQ 2017-18 Q4c (7 marks): Distinguish between muscle spasm and muscle cramp. What are the preventive measures?
FeatureMuscle SpasmMuscle Cramp
DefinitionInvoluntary, sustained muscle contraction — usually protective/reflexiveSudden, painful involuntary contraction — usually during/after exercise
CauseMuscle overuse, nerve irritation, injury, prolonged poor postureElectrolyte imbalance (Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺), dehydration, overuse, poor blood flow
DurationCan last hours/days (chronic back spasm)Seconds to minutes; self-limiting
PreventionErgonomic job design, rest breaks, stretching, avoiding sustained posturesAdequate hydration, electrolyte replenishment, warm-up/cool-down, gradual training progression

Chapter Summary

Key Takeaways

  1. EPOC: Extra O₂ post-exercise for PCr replenishment, lactate clearance, elevated temp, protein synthesis
  2. BMR affected by: body size, age, sex, composition, thyroid hormones, temperature, stress
  3. Blood to skin INCREASES during heavy work (thermoregulation); GI/renal flow decreases
  4. HR problems: Affected by heat, emotion, static work, medication — not purely work effort
  5. Murrell's formula: R = T(W−S)/(W−1.5) | S=5 kcal/min | rest=0 if W≤S
  6. MAP (VO₂max): Peaks at 20–25 yr; declines ~1%/yr; males 10–20% higher than females; safe sustained work ≤ 33% of MAP
  7. Overtime: Efficiency drops after ~50 hrs/week; rotating shifts cause circadian disruption
  8. Spasm vs Cramp: Spasm = reflexive/sustained (posture/injury); Cramp = electrolyte/hydration (exercise)

Previous Year Questions

2022-23★★★★★ · Q1a · 15 marks
(a) Describe the respiratory and cardiovascular responses to physical activity with necessary diagrams.
Cardiovascular response:
• HR rises linearly with VO₂ from ~70 bpm at rest to 220−age at max
• Stroke volume increases up to ~40–60% VO₂max, then plateaus
• Cardiac output = HR × SV; rises from ~5 L/min to ~20–25 L/min at max
• Blood redistribution: active muscles receive up to 85% of CO; skin blood flow increases for thermoregulation; GI and renal flow fall
• Blood pressure (systolic) rises; diastolic stays approximately constant or falls slightly (vasodilation in active muscles)

Respiratory response:
• Ventilation (VE) rises from ~6 L/min to ~100–150 L/min at maximum
• VE increases linearly with VO₂ up to anaerobic threshold (AT); above AT, VE rises steeply (ventilatory threshold = VT)
• Tidal volume increases first; then respiratory rate increases
• RER (VCO₂/VO₂): ~0.7 at rest (fat oxidation), 1.0 at AT, >1.0 above AT (extra CO₂ from bicarbonate buffering of lactate)
• Post-exercise: elevated VE and HR persist (EPOC) until homeostasis restored

Key diagrams to draw: (1) HR vs VO₂ linear plot with max HR indicated; (2) VE vs VO₂ showing linear phase then steep rise at AT; (3) Blood redistribution pie charts (rest vs heavy exercise)
2020-21 · 2014-15★★★★ · 2× · Q1a/Q1b · 15/20 marks
Describe the means of measuring physiological strain during physical work. What are their advantages and disadvantages?
Five methods:

1. Heart Rate: Chest strap or ECG. Adv: non-invasive, continuous, field-applicable, validated reference ranges (Brouha: HR at 1 min >110 bpm = work too heavy). Disadv: affected by heat, emotion, static work posture, caffeine, medication.

2. Oxygen Consumption (VO₂): Douglas bag / portable gas analyzer. Adv: direct energy measure, not influenced by stress/emotion, gold standard. Disadv: heavy equipment, restricts natural movement, lab conditions needed.

3. Electromyography (EMG): Surface electrodes on target muscles. Adv: localizes specific muscle loading, detects fatigue (median frequency drop), reveals static loading. Disadv: skin impedance, crosstalk, requires individual calibration, not easy in field.

4. Blood Lactate: Finger-prick, 3-minute intervals. Adv: directly quantifies anaerobic metabolism, defines AT (4 mmol/L). Disadv: invasive, discontinuous, blood-to-muscle lag, field impractical.

5. Perceived Exertion (Borg RPE 6–20): Self-report. Adv: simple, inexpensive, correlates with HR (RPE × 10 ≈ HR). Disadv: subjective, affected by worker motivation and reporting culture.
2023-24 · 2011-12★★★★ · 2× · Q7b/Q2b · 20/10 marks
(b) What are the factors that affect energy consumption during work?
Three categories of factors:

A. Task-Related:
• Workload: Force × distance — heavier lifts, longer carries = more energy
• Work rate/speed: Faster work is disproportionately more costly (non-linear)
• Posture: Awkward postures (stooped, kneeling, arms elevated) → 15–50% higher energy cost
• Type of work: Carrying > pushing > pulling for same load; dynamic > static (isometric)
• Muscle groups: Arm work less efficient than leg work for same external power

B. Worker-Related:
• Body weight: Higher weight → more energy for weight-bearing tasks
• Fitness (VO₂max): Fit workers handle same task at lower relative cost
• Age: Older workers: lower VO₂max → same task at higher % capacity
• Sex: Females have lower absolute capacity but similar relative (% capacity)
• Skill: Experienced workers use less energy (better coordination, less co-contraction)

C. Environmental:
• Heat/humidity: More blood to skin → competing with muscles; higher HR
• Cold: Shivering adds energy cost; heavy clothing restricts movement
• Altitude: Lower PO₂ → higher ventilation and HR for same O₂ delivery
2013-14 · 2010-11★★★ · 2× · Q7c/Q6c · 15/5 marks
What is Maximum Aerobic Power (MAP)? How is it related to age and sex?
Maximum Aerobic Power (MAP) = VO₂max = the maximum volume of oxygen the body can consume per unit time; the ceiling of aerobic energy production.

Measurement: Progressive exercise test (ergometer/treadmill) to voluntary exhaustion; VO₂ is measured until it plateaus despite increasing work rate.
Units: L O₂/min (absolute) or mL O₂/kg/min (relative — better for comparing workers of different sizes).
Typical values: Sedentary male: 35–45 mL/kg/min; Trained male: 55–70; Female: 10–20% lower at same training level.

Age relationship:
• VO₂max peaks at age 20–25 years
• Declines ~1% per year after age 25 regardless of activity level
• Decline due to: lower max HR (220−age), reduced stroke volume, decreased muscle mass, lower mitochondrial density
• By age 65, VO₂max is typically ~40% lower than at peak

Sex relationship:
• Males have ~10–20% higher absolute VO₂max
• Reasons: Greater cardiac output (larger heart, higher stroke volume), higher hemoglobin concentration, lower body fat %, greater lean muscle mass
• When expressed relative to fat-free mass, the difference narrows significantly

Occupational significance: Safe sustained work should not exceed 33% of VO₂max for an 8-hour shift.
2015-16 · 2013-14★★★ · 2× · Q6b/Q3a · 10 marks
How do overtime and shift work influence worker efficiency?
Shift Work Effects:
• Night shifts: Circadian rhythm desynchronization → alertness is lowest at 3–5 AM when night shift workers are most active → higher error rates, slower reaction times, increased accident risk
• Rotating shifts: Body cannot adapt (rotation too fast to fully re-entrain) → chronic sleep deficit → 2–4 hours less sleep per 24-hour period → accumulating cognitive and physical impairment
• Health effects: GI disorders (irregular meal times), cardiovascular disease, reproductive problems, psychological stress from social disruption

Overtime Effects:
• For moderate extension (up to ~48 hrs/week): productivity per hour remains near normal
• Beyond 50 hrs/week: output per hour declines — fatigue-induced errors increase; more rework → effective productivity drops below the overtime input
• Cumulative fatigue: insufficient recovery between shifts → performance degradation compounds across the week
• Long-term: chronic overwork → burnout, musculoskeletal disorders, increased absenteeism

Recommendation: Ergonomic scheduling — fixed shifts preferred over rotating; adequate recovery time (11+ hours between shifts); maximum 48 hrs/week work time.
2010-11★★★ · ~10 marks · Murrell Numerical
A worker lifts 20 kg repeatedly, with a height change of 20 inches (40" to 60"), at a rate of 15 lifts per minute. The metabolic cost of this work is 4 g-cal per ft-lb of mechanical work done. The standard energy expenditure limit is 5 kcal/min and resting metabolic rate is 1.5 kcal/min. Calculate the required rest period per hour using Murrell's formula.
Murrell's Rest Period Formula:
R = T(W − S) / (W − 1.5)
Where: R = rest time (min); T = total work period (min); W = work metabolic rate (kcal/min); S = standard limit = 5 kcal/min; 1.5 = resting metabolic rate (kcal/min)

Step 1 — Mechanical work per lift:
Load = 20 kg = 44.1 lbs; Height change = 20 inches = 1.667 ft
Work/lift = 44.1 × 1.667 = 73.5 ft-lb

Step 2 — Metabolic energy per lift:
= 73.5 ft-lb × 4 g-cal/ft-lb = 294 g-cal = 0.294 kcal (1 g-cal = 0.001 kcal)

Step 3 — Metabolic rate from lifting (at 15 lifts/min):
W_lift = 0.294 × 15 = 4.41 kcal/min

Step 4 — Total metabolic rate during work:
W = W_lift + W_basal = 4.41 + 1.5 = 5.91 kcal/min

Step 5 — Check: W > S? 5.91 > 5.0 → Yes, rest is required.

Step 6 — Apply Murrell's formula (T = 60 min):
R = 60 × (5.91 − 5.0) / (5.91 − 1.5)
R = 60 × 0.91 / 4.41
R = 12.4 minutes of rest per hour

Conclusion: Worker requires ~12.4 min rest per hour. Net productive work = 60 − 12.4 = 47.6 min/hour.
Redesign recommendation: Provide mechanical assist (conveyor/hoist) to reduce lifting frequency below 10/min and bring W below 5 kcal/min, eliminating rest requirement.
Exam — Brouha Criterion★★ · short question · ~5 marks
Explain the Brouha recovery pulse criterion (3-pulse test) for evaluating physical workload. What does it indicate?
Brouha 3-Pulse Test — Procedure:
After the worker stops work, heart rate is counted for 30 seconds at:
• P1 = pulse at 1–1.5 min post-work
• P2 = pulse at 2–2.5 min post-work
• P3 = pulse at 3–3.5 min post-work
(Values expressed as beats per 30 seconds × 2 = bpm, or directly as 30-sec counts)

Interpretation Criteria:
• P1 > 110 bpm: Work is too heavy — energy demand exceeded aerobic capacity; workload must be reduced
• P3 > 90 bpm: Recovery is incomplete — cumulative cardiovascular fatigue is occurring across the shift
• P3 > P2 > P1 (or P3 > P1): Heart rate is NOT declining after work — severe cardiovascular strain; immediate job redesign required
• P1 ≤ 110, P3 ≤ 90, P3 < P1: Work is acceptable — normal cardiac recovery pattern

Why it works: Recovery HR reflects both the intensity of work just completed AND the cumulative fatigue state of the cardiovascular system. A worker who cannot recover by 3 min post-work is chronically overloaded.

Advantages: Non-invasive, requires only a stopwatch, applicable in any field setting, accounts for recovery capacity not just peak HR.
Limitations: Affected by heat, emotion, medications, caffeine; does not directly measure energy expenditure (VO₂); influenced by static holding postures (high HR, low metabolic cost).
